title: Camp 2 close: the story you're in
hook: parables, a birth, a road, a cross, an empty tomb, a church on the move

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan of Arc, nineteen, facing her judges. Your line was I am not afraid. Did you say your one true thing? Today, the last day of the stories. Day ninety-six.

Seventy-five days ago, we started telling stories. Think back. A farmer throwing seed on every kind of ground. A woman sweeping the whole house for one coin. A servant who buried his talent because he was afraid. A young woman in Nazareth saying, let it be. A feeding trough. Shepherds on the night shift. Fishermen told to try the other side of the boat. A short man up a tree. A king on a donkey. A towel and a basin. A rooster. A cross. A garden, and a name said kindly. Then a road to Emmaus, a charcoal fire, wind and flame, a jailer, a shipwreck, a letter full of names. And saints: a mother's tears, a garden in Milan, birds, a wagon in the rain, a girl in armor.
screen: `SEED, COIN, TALENT.` → `A TROUGH, A CROSS, A GARDEN.` → `A FIRE, A FLAME, A SHIPWRECK.`

segments.voice: Mark's Gospel, the shortest, begins like this, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The beginning. Gospel is the old English godspel, good news, translating the Greek euangelion. Christians have always told it first as a story, not a list of ideas: parables that turn things upside down, a birth in the wrong place, a road through Galilee, one last week in Jerusalem, a cross, and an empty tomb. And here's the thing about the book of Acts, where this camp has lived for weeks. It doesn't end. The last scene has Paul under house arrest in Rome for two whole years, welcoming everyone who came to him, teaching, as Luke puts it, with all confidence, no man forbidding him. And then Luke stops. We never read Paul's trial or his death in Acts. The story is left open, mid-sentence. Christians have long read that open ending as deliberate: the story keeps going. Through Stephen and Philip and Lydia, then Monica and Augustine, Francis, Teresa, Joan, and millions of names nobody wrote down. Christians say every life that takes it up becomes another page. That doesn't mean anyone here has to believe it. Some of you are on this path because it's your faith, some because it's someone else's you love, some just to understand. But you've walked the whole length of it now, from the sower to the shipwreck. You know the stories. And the next part of this path moves from stories to practices: how Christians actually pray, sing, rest and live it, day to day. Camp three begins tomorrow. You're in the story now.
screen: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.` · `ACTS ENDS MID-SENTENCE.` · `ANOTHER PAGE, AND ANOTHER.` · `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICES.` · then, large: `YOU'RE IN THE STORY NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line of your own story. Sit, and breathe. Of all the stories in this camp, which one stayed with you? Don't think too hard: the first one that comes. Now ask where it touches your own life. Maybe you've been the lost coin. Maybe you're the one up the tree. Maybe you're on the road to Emmaus, sad, not recognizing something beside you. Find one sentence that says it. If you can, write it down now. If you pray, you can offer that sentence to God. The bell holds the time.
Camp two, closed. Parable, leaven, talent, annunciation, Magnificat, manger, baptism, disciple, the keys, transfiguration, hosanna, Pentecost, martyr, conversion, Gentile, epistle, agape, saint.
Your line: you're in the story now. Today, tell one person one of these stories, in your own words. Tomorrow, camp three opens with what prayer is. Day ninety-six.

howItsDone: Christians retell these stories every year through the church calendar, from the annunciation and Christmas through Holy Week, Easter and Pentecost, and remember the saints on their feast days. Many churches read the Gospels and Acts in order across the year.

fork.setup: you're Luke, finishing Acts. Paul is in Rome under house arrest, teaching everyone who comes. how do you end the book?
options: with a summary of everything he taught.
mid-story: Paul teaching, no man forbidding him.
fork.reveal: Luke stops with Paul teaching with all confidence, no man forbidding him. many Christians read the open ending as deliberate: the story keeps going.

original.note: Greek: good news. The old English godspel, gospel, translates it.

trapdoor: what you thought: seventy-five days of Bible stories.
what it means: one long story, from parables to a cross and an empty tomb to a church on the move, told as a story that stays open.
what a scholar hears: euangelion was a word for public good news, like a victory announcement; Acts 28 ends without Paul's trial, and scholars still debate why.

notes: Camp close: the hook retraces camp two, the word segment names the camp's words from the outline (parable, leaven, talent, annunciation, Magnificat, manger, baptism, disciple, the keys, transfiguration, hosanna, Pentecost, martyr, conversion, Gentile, epistle, agape, saint), and the carry points to camp three.
The teach says plainly that no one on the path has to believe the story; confirm this sits well with the index carry 'you're in the story now'.

'Euangelion was a word for public good news, like a victory announcement' (e.g., the Priene inscription): confirm.
